title: Gettysburg

jokes.text: Oh, my God, kill me
jokes.setup: A dry, bureaucratic reading of the Sabre Code of Conduct has just begun
jokes.punchline: An employee immediately responds with 'Oh, my God, kill me' — the most extreme possible reaction to corporate policy-reading
jokes.explanation: A relatable opener that efficiently sets the tone. The extreme hyperbole ('kill me') against the mundane corporate backdrop lands well. Not deeply original but executed with good economy.

jokes.text: Hey. All right, obviously we all want to die, but we have to get through this
jokes.setup: Andy is supposed to be the enthusiastic regional manager rallying his team
jokes.punchline: He immediately validates their death wish and just asks them to power through it anyway
jokes.explanation: Andy's eager-to-please manager persona making an accidental concession that undercuts his own authority. The joke works because it's so honest — he's trying to be a good manager but can't pretend the Code of Conduct isn't deadly dull.

jokes.text: Oh, is it okay with you? Because if it's not, you work for me, so...
jokes.setup: Andy tells Gabe it's 'okay' to proceed with reading the Code of Conduct
jokes.punchline: Gabe — who is widely regarded as having no real authority — asserts his technical organizational seniority over Andy with a passive-aggressive power play
jokes.explanation: Perfect Gabe characterization — simultaneously pathetic and technically correct. The joke lands because it exposes the absurdity of corporate hierarchy while being completely in-character for Gabe's desperate need to assert relevance.

jokes.text: I'm going into labor [used as an excuse to exit the Code of Conduct reading]
jokes.setup: The Code of Conduct reading is unbearable; Pam is visibly pregnant
jokes.punchline: Pam fakes going into labor as an escape — then the joke is that it works
jokes.explanation: Good use of Pam's pregnancy as a comedic device. The payoff is better than the setup — the fact that it actually works and everyone panics is the real laugh. Sets up the false-alarm callback.

jokes.text: I know it's wrong to fake going into labor just to get out of things, but sometimes it's necessary. [confessional] 'I'm going into labor' / 'But should I have corn dogs or...' / 'I'm going into labor' / 'Okay, three reasons you are wrong about True Blood. Number one — I'm going into labor'
jokes.setup: Pam confesses she uses fake labor as a get-out-of-anything card, then demonstrates with three absurd examples
jokes.punchline: The escalating mundanity of what she uses it to escape — corn dog decisions, True Blood debates — peaks with using it mid-argument as Point #1 in a rebuttal
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional construction. Three examples that escalate in absurdity (corn dogs → True Blood → using it as a logical argument point) is tight, rhythmic comedy writing. 'Three reasons you are wrong about True Blood. Number one — I'm going into labor' is the standout line, using a comedic structure (numbered list) and immediately demolishing it. Strong character specificity — this is distinctly Pam.

jokes.text: Hey guys, you can't keep saying you're going into labor. Everyone knows you're full of it.
jokes.setup: Pam has used 'I'm going into labor' as a joke repeatedly; Jim calls it out
jokes.punchline: Immediately after Jim says this, Pam IS actually in labor
jokes.explanation: Classic 'cry wolf' reversal executed with excellent timing. The structure is nearly perfect — Jim's speech about it being fake IS the setup, making his line the thing that triggers the real event. The 'Oh. Oh! Oh my gosh. Oh my God, Pam' reaction sells it. Strong rewatch value because it's a textbook-perfect callback payoff.

jokes.text: False alarm [title card / cut]
jokes.setup: The office has erupted in chaos getting Pam to the hospital
jokes.punchline: A cold cut to 'False alarm' — the joke is entirely in the brevity of the title card deflating all that drama
jokes.explanation: A structural joke — the comedy is entirely in the editing choice. The dramatic exit followed by an immediate 'False alarm' is a perfectly economical undercut. High economy score because there are literally two words doing all the work.

jokes.text: Customers, clients, it's like a war out there. I am a leader, but you can only inspire people so much in a place like this. So today, I'm turning the inspire factor up to 10 — with a little help from my friend, America's bloodiest battle.
jokes.setup: Andy frames losing a client as 'business is war' and announces a grand solution
jokes.punchline: His 'friend' is Gettysburg — America's most devastating military catastrophe — presented as a routine morale booster
jokes.explanation: Good premise setup for the episode. 'Turning the inspire factor up to 10 with a little help from my friend, America's bloodiest battle' is a well-constructed sentence that earns a laugh by treating mass death as a productivity hack. Functional episode-establishing comedy.

jokes.text: Why even read business books? We should be studying war.
jokes.setup: Andy is pitching the Gettysburg trip in a confessional
jokes.punchline: He delivers this as a profound insight — the joke is the confidence with which he states something deeply impractical
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Andy's unearned confidence in bad ideas. The line works but doesn't rise above functional. It's setting up the episode premise more than landing a big joke.

jokes.text: The Civil War history industry has conveniently forgotten about the Battle of Schrute Farms.
jokes.setup: The group is discussing going to Gettysburg, with Oscar noting it's actually the northernmost Civil War battle
jokes.punchline: Dwight introduces his competing claim — that a battle on his own family farm was more significant — and frames the official record as a conspiracy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best premises — Dwight believing his family farm had a Civil War battle that historians have conspired to suppress is quintessential Dwight Schrute. It's deeply character-specific (only Dwight would do this), introduces a running gag with major payoff potential, and 'the Civil War history industry' is a brilliantly paranoid turn of phrase. Scores high on originality and character integration because no other character on television would credibly deliver this line.

jokes.text: Whatever, I'm over it. It's just grossly irresponsible.
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Oscar) has corrected Dwight's claim about northernmost battles
jokes.punchline: Dwight says he's 'over it' and then immediately contradicts himself by calling it 'grossly irresponsible' — he is clearly not over it
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Dwight's wounded dignity is visible in the contradiction. 'Grossly irresponsible' applied to a historical record dispute is a nice overstatement.

jokes.text: And is anyone kosher or halal? / What's the halal option? / Dates, tabouleh and bagel with cream cheese. / Out. / You know, it's the same as the kosher option. There's a lesson in there.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to be inclusive about dietary restrictions for the trip
jokes.punchline: The halal option is identical to the kosher option; Andy notes 'there's a lesson in there' as if he's discovered profound interfaith wisdom through sandwich planning
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurdist specificity of the halal option (dates, tabouleh AND a bagel with cream cheese) and Andy's earnest discovery of interfaith common ground through lunch prep. 'There's a lesson in there' is a perfect mock-profound button.

jokes.text: I mean, I can't force you to go. You're not my slaves. Thanks to Gettysburg.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to recruit people for the Gettysburg trip
jokes.punchline: He catches himself after 'not my slaves' and adds 'Thanks to Gettysburg' — a historically accurate but deeply awkward aside
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark comedy — the self-correction makes the original slip worse, not better. 'Thanks to Gettysburg' as a three-word addendum lands with the right cringe-but-clever tone. It's funny because it's technically true and historically literate while being completely socially inept. Andy-specific awkwardness executed well.

jokes.text: Anyone who's not going, you're dead to me. You're uninvited. I don't want you to come. But FYI, there will be leftover turkey and pesto sammies in the fridge.
jokes.setup: Andy tries to make the Gettysburg trip sound exclusive and important
jokes.punchline: His tough-guy exclusion speech immediately collapses into a reminder about free food — revealing that he desperately wants everyone to come and can't actually follow through on any threat
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy — his threats have no teeth and he immediately undermines himself. The structure is good: ascending pressure ('dead to me / uninvited / don't want you to come') that drops instantly to 'pesto sammies.' The word 'sammies' does extra work making him sound even less threatening.

jokes.text: Phyllis, think fast! [throws sandwich at Phyllis]
jokes.setup: Andy is distributing lunches to people joining the trip
jokes.punchline: He throws a sandwich at Phyllis with no warning — presumably hitting her or nearly hitting her — a completely unnecessary action from a manager distributing food
jokes.explanation: Weak physical gag. The 'think fast' trope is lazy, and while it has minor Andy-as-oblivious-manager energy, it's mostly cheap slapstick without strong comedic purpose. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: All right, guys, a little foreplay before we do it. Fans of Ken Burns' Jazz will most certainly enjoy The Civil War.
jokes.setup: Andy is preparing the group on the bus for a Civil War documentary
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'foreplay' (mild sexual innuendo in a work context) and then pitches the documentary with an incorrect comparison — Ken Burns' Jazz and The Civil War are different documentaries, but Andy reverses the causality absurdly
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny but not sharply constructed. The 'foreplay' comment is the better half; the Ken Burns comparison is obtuse in a way that reads more as character confusion than purposeful comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, isn't that the one where the guy becomes limitless?
jokes.setup: Someone suggests watching Limitless on the bus instead of the documentary
jokes.punchline: Someone asks a perfectly literal question about the movie's plot as if it's a genuine inquiry — the joke is the stunning obviousness of the question (the movie is CALLED Limitless)
jokes.explanation: Quick, punchy observational joke. The comedy is in confirming what the title already tells you, delivered straight. Economy is the strength here — it's one sentence and it lands.

jokes.text: It's just not appropriate. If we were going to visit Bradley Cooper's birthplace, I'd be the first one suggesting it, I'd be rooting for it... Limitless, Limitless, Limitless, Limitless, Limitless!
jokes.setup: Andy refuses to let the group watch Limitless, invoking appropriateness
jokes.punchline: He then qualifies his opposition by saying he would fully support watching it if they were at Bradley Cooper's birthplace — a completely insane hypothetical — and then gets outvoted and cracks anyway
jokes.explanation: The Bradley Cooper's birthplace caveat is the funny part — a completely unnecessary and specific qualification that reveals Andy thinks in absurdly conditional terms. His capitulation ('Limitless, Limitless...') is a nice physical beat too.

jokes.text: By not going on the trip you've shown you're the free thinkers of the office. Robert, you've got your sheep and you got your black sheep. And I'm not even a sheep. I am on the freaking moon.
jokes.setup: Robert California arrives to find most of the office has left for Gettysburg; Dwight stayed behind
jokes.punchline: Dwight reframes his absence as intellectual superiority, escalating the sheep metaphor to being 'on the freaking moon' — beyond all categories
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight moment. The sheep/black sheep extended metaphor that he then explodes by placing himself on the moon is exactly the kind of grandiose self-mythology Dwight specializes in. 'I am on the freaking moon' is highly quotable and specific to the character. The escalation from metaphor to cosmic absurdity is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Game changers. Changes to the game such that the game can never be played the same way again.
jokes.setup: Robert California announces the brainstorming session topic
jokes.punchline: He defines 'game changers' tautologically — restating the compound word as its own definition with complete self-seriousness
jokes.explanation: Perfect Robert California — he speaks as if everything he says is profoundly illuminating when it's actually circular. Defining a compound noun by its component words with utter gravity is exactly his character's comedy mode. Only Robert California would deliver this as wisdom.

jokes.text: Don't be afraid to get weird with it. [pause] Meredith [pause]
jokes.setup: Robert encourages the group to brainstorm freely; the camera presumably cuts to Meredith
jokes.punchline: Robert singles out Meredith by name in a long pause — implying her response or expression to 'get weird with it' was notably alarming, given Meredith's well-established weirdness
jokes.explanation: A visual/reaction beat joke that plays perfectly in the mockumentary format. The word 'Meredith' alone, delivered after a pause, is the punchline — it implies her reaction to 'get weird' was concerning enough to warrant a direct address. Economy is exceptional (one word does all the work). Strong on rewatch because you can imagine exactly what Meredith did.

jokes.text: Fun fact: In France, they call Limitless 'The Man with Many Capabilities.'
jokes.setup: The group arrives at Gettysburg and Andy is trying to pivot them from the movie to the historical site
jokes.punchline: He offers a 'fun fact' about Limitless that is completely irrelevant to anything and also sounds made up — 'The Man with Many Capabilities' is a bureaucratically flat translation
jokes.explanation: Quietly excellent joke. The humor comes from the deadpan specificity of the fake French title — 'The Man with Many Capabilities' sounds exactly like an over-literal translation that deflates the movie's cool premise. Andy's delivery of it as a 'fun fact' adds another layer. Highly quotable standalone line.

jokes.text: I got Source Code on the way back.
jokes.setup: Andy has won the battle over Limitless vs. the documentary; the group is getting off the bus
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately plans the next movie resistance — they haven't even arrived yet and are already preparing to avoid the educational content on the return trip
jokes.explanation: Quick button on the Limitless running gag. Works as a capper — the group's resistance to education is total and preemptive. Not a big laugh but a nice rhythmic joke.

jokes.text: The Andy Bernard Tour... After Chancellorsville, Lee brought his army up the Shenandoah Valley right through here. They stopped in this field for a picnic, which they called 'lunch.'
jokes.setup: Andy insists on giving his own tour rather than going to the Visitors' Center, claiming he has 'meticulously researched' it
jokes.punchline: His historical narration reveals that his research amounts to: they stopped for a picnic — 'which they called lunch' — an explanation so obvious it borders on insane
jokes.explanation: This is a great joke. 'They stopped in this field for a picnic, which they called lunch' is the reveal that Andy's 'meticulous research' is essentially nothing. The parenthetical explanation of a word everyone knows ('which they called lunch') is the specific comic move that elevates this from a simple 'bad tour guide' joke to something quotably absurd.

jokes.text: Total deaths belongs to Gettysburg, but when you're talking about DPA — that's deaths per acre — nothing beats the Battle of Schrute Farms.
jokes.setup: Dwight is promoting the Battle of Schrute Farms over Gettysburg
jokes.punchline: He introduces 'DPA' (deaths per acre) as a legitimate competing metric — a completely invented statistic — delivered with the confidence of an expert citing peer-reviewed data
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. 'DPA — deaths per acre' is a perfectly constructed absurdist invention: it sounds like a real metric, it has an acronym, and the parenthetical definition ('that's deaths per acre') mimics how a real expert would introduce a technical term. The specificity of per-acre as the chosen denominator is exactly the kind of pedantic detail Dwight would fixate on. This is among the episode's best constructed jokes — deeply character-specific and wholly original.

jokes.text: And you should read some of these letters that the soldiers wrote home. I mean, it makes the Battle of Gettysburg sound like a bunch of schoolgirls wrestling over a hairbrush.
jokes.setup: Dwight is reading soldiers' letters to further prove Schrute Farms' superiority
jokes.punchline: His vivid dismissal of Gettysburg — 'a bunch of schoolgirls wrestling over a hairbrush' — is a completely unearned and oddly specific image
jokes.explanation: The simile is the joke — and 'schoolgirls wrestling over a hairbrush' is specific enough to be funny rather than generic. It's an absurd visual that Dwight delivers with complete sincerity. Good character work.

jokes.text: Really? Why don't you tell us the real history, Gore Vidal? / Okay, I will. I don't know who that is but I'm going to tell you this. He's a historian.
jokes.setup: Oscar sarcastically invokes Gore Vidal as a dig at Dwight's revisionist history claims
jokes.punchline: Dwight accepts the challenge completely seriously, admits he doesn't know who Gore Vidal is, and then Oscar flatly clarifies 'He's a historian' — Dwight has just declared he'll tell the history better than a historian, while not knowing who the historian is
jokes.explanation: Excellent three-beat exchange. Oscar's sarcastic reference, Dwight's oblivious acceptance of the challenge, and then Oscar's flat correction build a perfect small structure. 'I don't know who that is but I'm going to tell you this' followed by learning he's a historian (making the situation worse, not better) is tightly constructed comedy. The joke works on character: Dwight's confidence is impervious to information.

jokes.text: Was it the second most northern? [pause] Sure! I would cede it was the second most northern battle.
jokes.setup: Oscar and Dwight are arguing about whether Gettysburg was the northernmost Civil War battle; Dwight refuses to concede
jokes.punchline: Oscar asks sarcastically if it was at least the SECOND most northern, and Dwight — who has no evidence — immediately accepts this consolation prize as a real concession, using the word 'cede' as if this is a formal diplomatic negotiation
jokes.explanation: The use of 'cede' makes this joke. Dwight treating the second-northernmost-battle claim as a solemn territorial concession in a geopolitical dispute is exactly his character. Oscar's 'What?' reaction presumably carries visual comedy too.

jokes.text: Raw fish. The disgusting food from Japan that Americans would never want to eat. Now, we can't get enough of it. From movie stars to construction workers, sushi is what's for dinner.
jokes.setup: Robert California asks for game-changing innovations in a brainstorm; Kevin goes first
jokes.punchline: Kevin's pitch is... sushi. Already invented. Already mainstream. He delivers it as if he's uncovered a revolutionary trend that no one has noticed
jokes.explanation: Kevin pitching a decades-old food trend as a revolutionary innovation is perfectly in-character. 'Sushi is what's for dinner' is delivered with the cadence of someone who just cracked the code. The specificity of 'from movie stars to construction workers' signals that Kevin thinks this is breaking news. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Let me throw another idea at you. Origami. What? The crazy art of paper folding — from, that's right, Japan.
jokes.setup: Kevin has just pitched sushi as a game changer
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to origami, also from Japan, presented with the same breathless excitement — the joke being that he clearly just went down a mental 'cool Japanese things' list
jokes.explanation: The 'from — that's right — Japan' reveal is the specific funny beat. Kevin has clearly identified Japan as the source of all innovation and is working down a list. The buildup mimics an infomercial pitch voice, which is character-appropriate for Kevin's grandiosity about his bad ideas.

jokes.text: Don't you wish you could go back to 1980 and open the first sushi restaurant in Manhattan? We can do that with origami — it's the sushi of paper.
jokes.setup: Kevin is building his origami pitch
jokes.punchline: 'Origami — it's the sushi of paper' is Kevin's thesis statement, connecting two unrelated things as if it's a profound analogy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Origami — it's the sushi of paper' is a perfectly constructed absurdist analogy that sounds like it means something while meaning nothing. The structure (X is the Y of Z) mimics real marketing speak, which makes it funnier. It's highly quotable, works completely out of context, and is delivered with Kevin's signature oblivious confidence. The preceding setup ('go back to 1980 and open the first sushi restaurant') is also funny in its own right — Kevin conflating past opportunity with present invention.

jokes.text: This idea hasn't gripped me. What else did you come up with? / I had to memorize the presentation, Robert, and it took a long time to build the swan, so.
jokes.setup: Robert dismisses the origami pitch; Kevin apparently only prepared one idea
jokes.punchline: Kevin's defense is that he spent all his effort on memorization and swan-building — implying the full extent of his preparation was: learn the words, fold the paper. He has nothing else.
jokes.explanation: Robert's flat 'this idea hasn't gripped me' is perfectly in-character for his detached authority, and Kevin's defense ('it took a long time to build the swan') is both an excuse and an inadvertent self-burn. The trailing 'so' at the end is a nice comedic particle — Kevin knows he has nothing but refuses to accept it.

jokes.text: If your woman is like mine, I bet you come home to hear the same thing all the time: 'This paper is so hard. It scratches. Why can't there be a paper just for me?' Well, now there is. It's pink, scented and silky soft. Now you can watch the game and she can write a letter to her sister.
jokes.setup: The brainstorm continues; Meredith presents her idea
jokes.punchline: Meredith's 'game changer' is gendered stationery, framed in the most aggressively retrograde advertising voice imaginable — made funnier because it's MEREDITH, the least domestic, most aggressively unfeminine character on the show
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke is that Meredith — who is chaotic, hard-drinking, and the opposite of the 1950s housewife archetype — is pitching this as if she's identified a real gap in the market for ladylike stationery. 'Now you can watch the game and she can write a letter to her sister' is the best line, a comedically specific image of domestic separatism. High character integration because only Meredith pitching this is funny.

jokes.text: The situation you described — returning home to a wife complaining about her paper being too masculine — is not one that I'm familiar with. [pause] In the African American community.
jokes.setup: Meredith has pitched gendered paper to the group
jokes.punchline: Robert begins a standard dismissal, then adds a qualifying phrase — 'in the African American community' — that implies he's clarifying a cultural demographic point, which is either a non-sequitur or a deeply strange additional observation
jokes.explanation: Classic Robert California — he says something that sounds profound or authoritative but is actually bizarre and possibly inappropriate. The appended 'In the African American community' suggests he was qualifying his original statement to a specific demographic context, which raises more questions than it answers. The pause before the qualification is key. Strong character integration — Robert's unsettling non-sequiturs are a hallmark.

jokes.text: Thought it was worth a try.
jokes.setup: Robert has essentially dismissed Meredith's idea
jokes.punchline: Meredith accepts the rejection with a completely unsurprised, casual shrug — 'Thought it was worth a try' implies she knew it was probably a bad idea and pitched it anyway
jokes.explanation: A small button that works because of Meredith's character — she has zero ego investment. The economy is excellent but the joke itself is minor.

jokes.text: Can you tell us about the Battle of Schrute Farms? / Oh, I haven't heard of that one. / Really? Okay, follow-up question: how much are they paying you to keep your mouth shut?
jokes.setup: Dwight accosts a Gettysburg park guide about the Battle of Schrute Farms
jokes.punchline: When the guide says he hasn't heard of it, Dwight's immediate follow-up is to accuse the guide of being paid to stay silent — the conspiracy deepens in Dwight's mind with every piece of contrary evidence
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the Schrute Farms conspiracy. The logical structure is impeccable from a comedic standpoint: guide's ignorance → proof of conspiracy → bribery accusation. 'How much are they paying you to keep your mouth shut?' as a 'follow-up question' is pitch-perfect. Only Dwight processes disconfirming evidence as confirmation. The word 'follow-up' giving it a professional veneer makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I apologize for my friend. And for the Republicans who are cutting your funding.
jokes.setup: Oscar is apologizing to the park guide for Dwight's conspiracy accusation
jokes.punchline: He pivots from a reasonable apology to a political dig at Republicans — two completely unrelated offenses being apologized for in the same breath
jokes.explanation: Good Oscar characterization — he can't resist a political jab even while trying to smooth over an awkward situation. The structure works because the apology format sets up the expectation of diplomacy which the second clause undermines. Very Oscar-specific.

jokes.text: Apparently, I bear a passing resemblance to Abraham Lincoln. It makes it kind of hard for me to go to places like museums, historical monuments... elementary schools.
jokes.setup: A child calls out 'Are you Lincoln?' at Gettysburg, and Andy has to explain his Lincoln resemblance
jokes.punchline: The list of places it makes 'hard' to go escalates from expected (museums, monuments) to strange (elementary schools) — the last item implies something specific and uncomfortable about children recognizing a man as Lincoln
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'elementary schools' is the joke — it raises the uncomfortable implication that a Lincoln lookalike causes specific problems at schools (presumably children swarm him demanding Lincoln performances). The rule of three works well: two expected items, one odd one. The 'I don't see it' reaction presumably comes from Jim or someone else, which is a nice button.

jokes.text: I don't see it. [reaction to Andy's Lincoln resemblance]
jokes.setup: Andy explains he has a striking resemblance to Lincoln; the visual presumably makes it obvious he does
jokes.punchline: Jim flatly denies seeing the resemblance — presumably in a talking head or as a direct reaction — when contextually it's very clear Andy does look like Lincoln in this setting
jokes.explanation: Jim's deadpan denial is a solid reaction beat. Works on the mockumentary level — Jim would casually dismiss obvious things. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Chelsea, give Mr. Lincoln your hat so I can take a picture.
jokes.setup: A random tourist immediately accepts Andy as Abraham Lincoln
jokes.punchline: A stranger starts directing their child to cooperate with Andy's Lincoln performance — without asking, without hesitation — immediately recruiting Andy into a photo op as if he's a costumed actor
jokes.explanation: The joke is the tourist's complete presumption. Works as a setup for the escalating Lincoln bit but isn't strong on its own.

jokes.text: Hello, I'm Abraham Lincoln. Some people call me the 'Great Emancipator,' but you might know me from the penny.
jokes.setup: Andy has been forced/charmed into performing as Lincoln for the crowd
jokes.punchline: 'But you might know me from the penny' — Lincoln introducing himself via the penny is a perfect comedic anticlimax to 'Great Emancipator'
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The structure is classic anticlimax: big historical title ('Great Emancipator') → petty monetary association ('the penny'). The phrase 'you might know me from' mimics a celebrity introducing themselves by their most recognizable work, which makes the penny even funnier as Lincoln's 'credits.' Highly quotable, works completely out of context.

jokes.text: You know the test booklets they give out in all the schools? I was thinking that we could put a coupon in the back that people would mail in to us. And as, you know, as I tell it, I don't like it.
jokes.setup: The brainstorm session; Dwight pitches a game-changing idea to Robert California
jokes.punchline: He pitches a coupon-in-test-booklets idea and then — mid-sentence, in real time — talks himself out of it, concluding 'I don't like it' before he's even finished
jokes.explanation: Good joke. 'As I tell it, I don't like it' is the payoff — Dwight's real-time self-rejection while pitching is an unexpected comedic beat. It suggests he's pitching to test the idea rather than because he believes it, which is a subtle character insight delivered comedically.

jokes.text: Unless, of course, you are responding to it. / I am not.
jokes.setup: Robert offers Dwight an out — maybe the idea is good if he's reacting to something
jokes.punchline: Dwight flatly, immediately confirms: no, he really just doesn't like it
jokes.explanation: A clean button on the coupon joke. 'I am not' is functionally funny because of how definitive it is. The exchange is brief and works as a comedic capper.

jokes.text: At this point, when you're this pregnant, it's kind of like senior spring. The other day, I spit my gum out on the carpet.
jokes.setup: Pam is in a confessional about her late-stage pregnancy
jokes.punchline: She describes late pregnancy as 'senior spring' — the carefree time when consequences no longer apply — and illustrates it with spitting gum on the carpet, a completely minor transgression that she presents as wild rule-breaking
jokes.explanation: Charming and smart. 'Senior spring' is a perfect analogy for late pregnancy (a time when effort ceases because the end is in sight), and the illustration — spitting gum on the carpet — is precisely calibrated. It's a tiny act of rebellion that reveals Pam's personality: her version of going wild is something most people wouldn't notice. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: You know how in the vending machine, they have the chocolate chip cookies in the A-1 spot? They do that because they think A-1 is the best spot for the best cookie. But the real best spot is D-4. Right? That's where the eyes go.
jokes.setup: Robert asks Kevin for his game changer idea
jokes.punchline: Kevin's insight is about vending machine product placement — specifically that D-4 is the true prime real estate of a vending machine. He has clearly thought about this deeply.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's vending machine theory is wonderfully specific — he's identified D-4 as the prime visual real estate with the confidence of a retail analyst. The joke works because it's simultaneously idiotic (it's about snack placement) and internally coherent (the logic actually makes some sense). Kevin has clearly spent significant mental energy on this. Deep character integration — only Kevin would crack the vending machine code.

jokes.text: Yeah. But not just the cookies, though. That was just a for instance.
jokes.setup: Robert asks Kevin about cookie placement as if that's his actual pitch
jokes.punchline: Kevin clarifies that cookies were just a jumping-off point — there's a bigger theory underneath, which Robert immediately grasps and applies to Dunder Mifflin's product strategy
jokes.explanation: The setup for the Robert pivot. Functional but the humor is primarily in what comes next — Robert taking Kevin's vending machine metaphor seriously and applying it to business. Kevin's 'that was just a for instance' is a good detail though, implying he has a whole framework.

jokes.text: Who else agrees with Kevin that we're wasting facilities, manpower on our underselling products when we should be pushing our top performers?
jokes.setup: Kevin's cookie-placement idea has just been presented
jokes.punchline: Robert reframes Kevin's cookie placement as a serious business philosophy — finding genuine strategic insight in the most mundane possible source
jokes.explanation: Robert treating Kevin's vending machine observation as genuine business insight is a funny inversion — the smartest person in the room elevating the most food-focused. Works as both Robert character comedy and as a callback to Kevin's pitch.

jokes.text: There you get consensus. Okay, we are now on a planet where Kevin is the most creative person around and I am just some good-looking guy.
jokes.setup: Robert has just validated Kevin's vending machine insight as genuine business strategy; the room agrees
jokes.punchline: Robert processes what just happened — Kevin being the smartest person in the room — and his response is to note this as an alien reality ('a planet where...') and self-describe as 'just some good-looking guy'
jokes.explanation: Robert California's self-awareness delivered without self-pity. 'A planet where Kevin is the most creative person' frames the absurdity of the situation perfectly, and 'I am just some good-looking guy' is the disarming self-description of a man used to being the most interesting person in the room. The joke functions on character (Robert's ego acknowledging something impossible has occurred) and on economy.

jokes.text: I just don't understand. It's 1865, victory is ours. I have saved the very soul of our nation and yet, happiness eludes me. Oh, perhaps a trip to the theater will enliven my spirits.
jokes.setup: Andy, dressed as Lincoln, is performing for the growing crowd at Gettysburg
jokes.punchline: Andy-as-Lincoln arrives at the assassination joke — 'perhaps a trip to the theater' — which is the darkest possible punchline delivered with cheerful obliviousness
jokes.explanation: The assassination callback is well-constructed: the setup is Lincoln's post-war ennui (which is characterful), the punchline is the theater reference which the audience of 100 comedy-savvy viewers will catch before the in-universe crowd does. It's a dark joke that works because Andy delivers it completely earnestly. The 'No' reaction from someone in the crowd is a nice button.

jokes.text: So, another thing about oatmeal cookies. Who even wants them? I mean, I've seen Toby eat one, like, once. But other than that, forget it.
jokes.setup: Kevin's vending machine theory has pivoted to a business strategy metaphor; Kevin continues riffing
jokes.punchline: Kevin dismisses oatmeal cookies with forensic certainty — he has clearly surveilled Toby's cookie consumption closely enough to say 'once' — and 'Toby eating an oatmeal cookie' is the one documented case in Kevin's personal research
jokes.explanation: Kevin's specificity about Toby is what makes this joke — he has conducted informal empirical research and Toby is the only data point. The dismissive 'forget it' after establishing the Toby case is a good button. Also a gentle dig at Toby's sad office existence.

jokes.text: By the way, did we leave all the food on the bus? / Let's talk about food for a second. Food for thought. / Yeah, that's what I had for breakfast, and I think that's probably why I'm still hungry.
jokes.setup: Andy tries to make a grand speech about 'food for thought'; someone asks about the actual food on the bus
jokes.punchline: An employee responds to 'food for thought' literally — noting they had it for breakfast and it's not filling
jokes.explanation: Classic wordplay/literal interpretation joke. The 'food for thought' idiom taken literally is an old construct, but it's executed cleanly and the character's delivery ('that's probably why I'm still hungry') adds a self-pitying note that elevates it slightly.

jokes.text: Hunger for victory. Hunger for honor. Hunger for pride. / Hunger for hamburgers. / Hunger for chicken chimichangas.
jokes.setup: Andy is building an inspirational speech about hunger — for pride, honor, victory
jokes.punchline: Jim and Darryl immediately break the rhetorical mode with 'hunger for hamburgers' and 'hunger for chicken chimichangas' — Darryl's 'chicken chimichangas' is the funnier escalation of the two
jokes.explanation: The rhetorical escalation broken by literal hunger is a classic comedy move, but 'chicken chimichangas' as the escalation of 'hamburgers' is the specific funny detail — Darryl being more enthusiastic than Jim, and his specific food choice, adds character texture. Andy's 'Right, Darryl? That's good' accepting the chimichanga into his speech is also a nice beat.

jokes.text: I commissioned this flag for Dunder Mifflin. It cost me $200. / Only $200?
jokes.setup: Andy reveals the Dunder Mifflin flag he's had made as part of his battlefield inspiration speech
jokes.punchline: He presents $200 as a significant investment; someone's 'Only $200?' implies the flag looks cheap — and also that Andy spent his own money on a company flag for a battlefield exercise
jokes.explanation: The 'Only $200?' reaction is the joke — it implies the flag looks like $200 is too much, or that for a corporate flag it should be more, or both. Andy spending personal money on a company flag is a sad detail. Functional but not a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: Don't look where I am, look where I'm going. Jerk right, jerk left, jerk!
jokes.setup: Andy is running around Gettysburg with the Dunder Mifflin flag, trying to evade Jim in a mock flag battle
jokes.punchline: Andy's trash talk during the flag game is that of someone who takes the exercise extremely seriously — shouting football/basketball evasion cues on a Civil War battlefield
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy moment that works primarily visually — the spectacle of Andy running around a battlefield with a company flag while people are uncomfortable. 'Jerk right, jerk left' is funny sports-speak in the wrong context but it's not a crafted joke so much as a sustained bit.

jokes.text: Andy, this is inappropriate. People died here, man.
jokes.setup: Andy is running around Gettysburg with a company flag shouting trash talk
jokes.punchline: Jim's extremely measured, calm objection ('People died here, man') is the voice of reason delivered with such understatement that it becomes absurd
jokes.explanation: Jim's signature straight-man delivery. 'People died here, man' is such an obvious statement that it loops back to funny — of course people died there, it's Gettysburg. The 'man' at the end adds a weary exasperation.

jokes.text: Spangler's Spring is a mile this way. / Oh, wow. So, that's two miles if you incorporate the walk back.
jokes.setup: Dwight announces the next destination on the tour — a mile away
jokes.punchline: Someone calculates the round trip distance with the seriousness of a math problem, and presents 'two miles' as a revelation — as if they'd discovered something Dwight hadn't accounted for
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the unnecessary math: everyone knows a mile there and back is two miles. Presenting it as new information delivered with gravity is mildly funny. The 'incorporate the walk back' phrasing is good — 'incorporate' is the corporate word choice in the wrong context.

jokes.text: All I had for breakfast was oatmeal, yogurt, coffee, orange juice, and toast. Two poached eggs and then that half a sandwich on the bus. I can't.
jokes.setup: Someone claims they can't walk another mile because they haven't eaten enough
jokes.punchline: They list a substantial breakfast — oatmeal, yogurt, coffee, OJ, toast, TWO poached eggs, half a sandwich — while claiming it's insufficient. The list keeps going well past what any reasonable person would consider inadequate.
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of foods claimed as insufficient is the joke — each addition makes the complaint more absurd. 'Two poached eggs and then that half a sandwich on the bus' is the tipping point where it becomes ridiculous. The 'I can't' final beat is a good button.

jokes.text: I'm still going, and I'm not going to ask anymore. I'm just going to assume that you're with me. [walks off, pauses] / You said you weren't going to look back.
jokes.setup: Andy gives a determined speech about going forward without looking back
jokes.punchline: He immediately looks back; Jim calls it out flatly
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy setup/callback. Andy's speech setting up the promise and immediately breaking it is standard but executed cleanly with good economy. Jim's 'You said you weren't going to look back' is the precise straight-man button that makes it land.

jokes.text: And why is BlackRock suddenly the paragon by which all hedge funds must now be compared? / Yeah, I don't know. / Right? I mean, you're an accountant. Those bogus prospectuses must drive you insane. / Yes, I am an accountant.
jokes.setup: Robert California is trying to bond with Oscar over finance, asking about BlackRock
jokes.punchline: Oscar responds to Robert's intense question with 'Yeah, I don't know' and then, when Robert presses him as an accountant, his confirmation is the most deflated possible: 'Yes, I am an accountant' — acknowledging his identity rather than engaging with the content
jokes.explanation: Oscar — the most intellectually confident person in the office — responding to Robert California's financial intensity with 'Yeah, I don't know' is a perfect status joke. Robert assumes Oscar will match his energy; Oscar simply doesn't. 'Yes, I am an accountant' as a response to whether prospectuses drive him insane is brilliantly deflating — he's confirming he exists rather than engaging. Classic Robert California vs. reality interaction.

jokes.text: Well, anyone employed by the Gettysburg industrial complex is certainly going to want to keep quiet about the Battle of Schrute Farms.
jokes.setup: Oscar introduces an archivist at Gettysburg who might have records about Schrute Farms
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately pre-empts any credibility the archivist might have by accusing him of being part of 'the Gettysburg industrial complex' — an industry apparently dedicated to suppressing Schrute Farm history
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'Gettysburg industrial complex' is the star here — riffing on 'military-industrial complex,' Dwight has named an entire power structure dedicated to historical suppression of his family farm. It's the Schrute Farms running gag at its most committed and specific. The paranoia has its own internal logic. Strong rewatch value and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Families and sweethearts back home waited desperately for letters from the front. 'Dearest Mother, I'm sorry it has been so long since my last letter. It is three months since I arrived at Schrute Farms, and I fear I may never leave this place alive. Melvyn Fifer Garris.'
jokes.setup: The archivist has confirmed he's heard of Schrute Farms, and Dwight is triumphant — about to be validated
jokes.punchline: The letter's content seems to confirm the historical gravity of Schrute Farms... until we get the context of WHY in the next beat. The soldier's desperate letter is an effective emotional fake-out before the revelation.
jokes.explanation: This works as the setup to the major Schrute Farms payoff. 'Hallowed ground' is Dwight's interjection — premature celebration before the truth. The joke is structural here; the setup is a real emotional misdirection before the revelation that Schrute Farms was a refuge for artists, not soldiers.

jokes.text: But the battle at Schrute Farms was no battle at all. It was a code used by pacifists from both Norte and Soute, who'd turned the Pennsylvania farmhouse into an artistic community and a refuge from the war... poets, artists, dancers, these kinds of men preferred peace to war. These delicate, lovely men found a place of refuge among the Schrutes of Schrute Farm.
jokes.setup: Dwight has been insisting for the whole episode that Schrute Farms was the site of the most significant Civil War battle
jokes.punchline: The archivist reveals Schrute Farms was not a battlefield but a pacifist arts commune — 'poets, artists, dancers... delicate, lovely men' — directly undermining Dwight's warrior mythology about his own family
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of The Office's finer long-form gags. The entire Schrute Farms storyline has been building to this: Dwight's warrior family mythos is destroyed by the revelation that his ancestors ran a safe haven for 'delicate, lovely men' who preferred art to war. The irony is devastating for Dwight's self-image. It's earned (episode-long setup), original (the specific subversion of tough-guy heritage into arts commune), deeply character-specific, and economically delivered through a credible third party. 'Norte and Soute' and 'delicate, lovely men' are choice details. This is the episode's standout moment.

jokes.text: Amidst the macho brutality of war, this was a place where dandies and dreamers could put on plays, sing tender ballads and dance in the moonlight. I like to think of Schrute Farm as the Underground Railroad for the sensitive and, well, fabulous.
jokes.setup: The archivist is describing Schrute Farms as an arts commune
jokes.punchline: 'The Underground Railroad for the sensitive and, well, fabulous' — a perfectly constructed analogy that maximizes the contrast with Dwight's warrior mythology
jokes.explanation: The best single line of the episode. 'The Underground Railroad for the sensitive and, well, fabulous' is exceptional comedy writing: it takes a real historical reference (Underground Railroad), applies it to an unexpected demographic ('the fabulous'), and the pause before 'fabulous' ('and, well') adds a searching quality that makes it funnier. The phrase 'dandies and dreamers' is also exquisite. This line is what elevates the Schrute Farms payoff from merely good to genuinely outstanding television comedy. Extremely high quotability.

jokes.text: Wow, this is so much better than the story you made up.
jokes.setup: Dwight has just heard the true history of Schrute Farms — that it was a pacifist arts commune
jokes.punchline: Erin, who was fully taken in by Dwight's version earlier, now enthusiastically prefers the real story, completely missing the social grace of not pointing this out to Dwight's face
jokes.explanation: Erin's response is perfectly calibrated — her genuine enthusiasm for the real story is oblivious to how crushing it is for Dwight. 'So much better than the story you made up' is both complimentary and devastating. Classic Erin character comedy: she means well and lands poorly.

jokes.text: I've seen enough.
jokes.setup: Erin has just said the true Schrute Farms history is better than what Dwight made up; Dwight must process that his family mythology is destroyed
jokes.punchline: Dwight's three-word exit ('I've seen enough') is both comic deflation (the most dignified retreat he can muster) and a visual joke — he walks away from his own family's debunked legacy
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — three words deliver Dwight's entire emotional state. His dignified retreat while completely losing is quintessential Dwight. The understatement is enormous: 'I've seen enough' as a response to learning your warrior ancestors were actually dancing with poets. One of the better reaction beats of the episode.

jokes.text: You're right, there should be a monument to this.
jokes.setup: Dwight has just walked away humiliated from the Schrute Farms revelation
jokes.punchline: Oscar — who has been fighting Dwight all episode — cannot resist twisting the knife: endorsing a monument to the thing that destroyed Dwight's myth
jokes.explanation: Oscar delivering a final twist of the knife in Dwight's moment of defeat is perfectly in-character. The line is short and sharp. Works as a button on the Schrute Farms storyline.

jokes.text: Never trust a cookie with a woman's name. Pecan Sandy. Lorna Doone. Madeleine. Oh. They'll just break your heart.
jokes.setup: The oatmeal cookie/bad product running gag has been going on throughout the brainstorm
jokes.punchline: Kevin has developed a philosophy: cookies with women's names are untrustworthy. He lists three (Pecan Sandy, Lorna Doone, Madeleine), pauses meaningfully, and delivers 'They'll just break your heart' as if sharing hard-won romantic wisdom
jokes.explanation: This is excellent comedy writing. The conceit — applying romantic wisdom to cookies by name — is original, and 'They'll just break your heart' delivering cookie-buying advice as heartbreak wisdom is the perfect emotional mismatch. Kevin speaking with the voice of someone who has loved and lost, but about cookies. The list of three (Sandy, Lorna, Madeleine) is well-chosen — they do all sound like women who would disappoint you. The 'Oh' before the punchline is a nice breath that signals incoming wisdom. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Kevin, you are — [interrupted]
jokes.setup: Kevin has just delivered the 'never trust a cookie with a woman's name' philosophy
jokes.punchline: Robert California begins what would presumably be a compliment or profound statement about Kevin, but is cut off — the interrupted sentence is itself the joke, implying Robert has finally met his match in philosophical depth
jokes.explanation: The interrupted compliment works because Robert is usually the one ending conversations with profound inconclusiveness. Here it happens TO him. Functional as a button but not a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: I call it the Big Mac idea. / What? No. / Big Mac idea. Sounds encouraging. / It's really, really good, Robert. Let me explain. / No, this is not fair. This is my idea. He's trying to steal it because he's jealous of me.
jokes.setup: The brainstorm session; Dwight announces 'the Big Mac idea'
jokes.punchline: Kevin immediately reacts with 'What? No' — recognizing that Dwight is about to steal his idea — while Robert encouragingly says 'Sounds encouraging.' The simultaneous reactions create a comedic collision.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the three-way collision: Dwight confidently stealing, Kevin panicking, Robert obliviously encouraging. 'He's trying to steal it because he's jealous of me' is a great Kevin line — the wounded dignity of someone whose vending machine insight is being appropriated.

jokes.text: Every time you buy a Big Mac, you set one ingredient aside. Then, at the end of the week, you have a free Big Mac. And you love it even more because you made it with your own hands.
jokes.setup: Dwight is pitching the 'Big Mac idea' he stole from Kevin
jokes.punchline: The idea is insane: you can get a 'free' Big Mac by saving components over a week — ignoring that you paid for each ingredient, that the saved food would spoil, and that the assembled week-old Big Mac would be horrifying
jokes.explanation: The Big Mac idea is a great absurdist premise: a 'clever' scheme that falls apart on even minimal scrutiny, delivered with complete conviction. 'And you love it even more because you made it with your own hands' is the line that makes it — the emotional payoff of eating a week-old deconstructed burger is presented as a feature, not a bug. It also doesn't apply to paper sales in any way, which makes it funnier as a 'game changer.'

jokes.text: You know what? Now I remember. That was your idea. / That is 100% your idea.
jokes.setup: Kevin protests that Dwight stole his idea
jokes.punchline: Robert and Dwight both suddenly 'remember' the idea is Kevin's — an immediate and complete reversal motivated purely by the idea turning out to be bad or embarrassing
jokes.explanation: The instant abandonment of the Big Mac idea the moment it's attributed back to Kevin is a nice reversal. Both Robert and Dwight's certainty — 'Now I remember' / '100% your idea' — is funny in its definitiveness. Classic workplace comedy about credit and blame.

jokes.text: Oh, my [pause]. It was just actually cookies the whole time.
jokes.setup: The entire brainstorm session has ended; Robert processes what happened
jokes.punchline: Robert California — who claimed to be looking for game-changing innovations — realizes the only useful idea was Kevin's vending machine cookie theory, which IS literally just about cookies
jokes.explanation: Excellent button on the entire B-plot. Robert California, who speaks exclusively in profound abstractions, arriving at 'it was just actually cookies the whole time' is a perfect puncturing of his own pomposity. The pause before it ('Oh, my [pause]') suggests he's computing something significant. The joke is that the most banal possible truth (cookies) has emerged from his rarefied brainstorming exercise.

jokes.text: Damn it. Hey!
jokes.setup: Kevin has just been given back credit for the 'Big Mac idea' and realizes it's actually terrible
jokes.punchline: Kevin's 'Damn it' acknowledges he's been out-maneuvered (he has 'won' credit for a bad idea) and his 'Hey!' is presumably catching someone trying to slip away — a double-take beat
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/reaction beat. Kevin realizing he's been double-crossed into owning a bad idea is a nice moment. Mostly physical.

jokes.text: Phyllis is sitting on the ground eating a dirty sandwich.
jokes.setup: Jim reports back on the state of the people left at the bus
jokes.punchline: The specific image of Phyllis on the ground eating a dirty sandwich is the entire joke — a comedic dispatch that paints a picture of resigned, defeated energy
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'dirty sandwich' and Phyllis on the ground creates a vivid, sad image that's funnier than any elaboration would be. It's a perfectly economical visual gag delivered verbally. The comedy is in the resigned dignity — Phyllis is going to eat that sandwich.

jokes.text: Yeah, I asked the bus driver to lock it because our stuff was in there. I guess he follows orders.
jokes.setup: People are locked out of the bus; they ask why
jokes.punchline: Andy's defensive explanation ends with 'I guess he follows orders' — a passive-aggressive observation that the bus driver is more obedient than Andy's own staff, while simultaneously revealing Andy's management style created this
jokes.explanation: The dig — 'I guess he follows orders' — is a passive-aggressive note about his own staff's insubordination, made funnier by the fact that Andy is obviously the one who created the problem. Self-revealing character comedy.

jokes.text: Our office has a disease, and it goes by many names. Sarcasm, snark, 'wisecracks.' You take things that people care about and you make them feel lame about it with your jokes. That's what you did with this trip.
jokes.setup: Jim confronts Andy about the failed Gettysburg trip and its reception
jokes.punchline: Jim — the most sarcastic, wisecracking character on the show, famous for his camera looks and quips — delivers a speech about how sarcasm is a disease that hurts people. The meta-irony is enormous.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional meta-comedy. Jim Halpert — whose entire character arc on The Office is built on being the sarcastic, ironic straight-man who quips at everything — delivering a sincere speech about how sarcasm and wisecracks are a 'disease' is deeply self-referential. The show is critiquing its own comedy voice through its most comedic character, while playing it completely straight. It works as genuine character growth AND as a meta-joke that comedy-savvy viewers will catch. High marks for originality (the show interrogating its own mode), structure (set up against Jim's own character), and character integration (only Jim delivering this creates the irony).

jokes.text: Andy, if you don't believe me, take a look at what's on my head. I'm wearing a very pink hat. I've been getting weird looks all day, because I'm pretty sure 'DM does GB' means something kind of sexual. But guess who's wearing them? All of us. Just for you, man. That's huge.
jokes.setup: Jim is telling Andy that the team cares about him as a manager even if they didn't engage with the trip
jokes.punchline: 'DM does GB' as potentially sexual, and the commitment to wearing embarrassing pink hats all day at Gettysburg as proof of loyalty — the comedy is in the specific embarrassment Jim has endured to make this point
jokes.explanation: 'DM does GB' as sexual innuendo is a nice throwaway joke in a sincere speech — it says something about Jim that he noticed this immediately and still wore the hat. The emotional sincerity doesn't undercut the comedy; it enriches it. Good character integration — Jim's willingness to be earnest is a key late-series trait.

jokes.text: You don't like the hats? / They're terrible. / I hate myself.
jokes.setup: Andy asks about the hats his team has been wearing all day
jokes.punchline: Jim confirms they're terrible, and Andy's self-flagellation ('I hate myself') is the instant collapse of any remaining dignity
jokes.explanation: 'I hate myself' as Andy's response to learning the hats are bad is pure Andy — immediate self-punishment. The exchange is economical and lands cleanly. 'They're terrible' from Jim is also good because he admits it so readily after his entire speech about them being a gesture of loyalty.

jokes.text: The world will little note nor long remember the fight that Jim and I had here at Gettysburg. And that's good, because I was basically wrong. I wanted my team to be like this army and I was their general. But I guess it's really just more like they're people who work in an office and I'm their manager. Yeah, that's really probably a better analogy. Now that I think about it.
jokes.setup: Andy delivers an end-of-episode confessional about his Gettysburg lesson
jokes.punchline: He opens with a Gettysburg Address parody ('The world will little note nor long remember') and then gently walks back his entire war metaphor to its obvious mundane truth — they work in an office, he's their manager — with 'Yeah, that's really probably a better analogy' as a sheepish aside
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured episode button. The Gettysburg Address echo ('The world will little note...') applied to a minor manager-employee argument is the right scale of irony. Andy's conclusion that 'people who work in an office' and 'manager' are probably better analogies than 'army' and 'general' is delivered with the earnestness of someone who just figured this out. 'Now that I think about it' is a perfect comedic trailing qualifier — he's landing on obvious truth as if it's new insight.

jokes.text: Abe and Mary are seated watching the show. / Oh, Mary, this is wonderful. / Okay, Mary, stop your scolding. I'll be quiet. / I need her like I need a hole in the head. / [Bang!]
jokes.setup: Andy, still in Lincoln mode, has apparently watched the performance/show with a woman playing Mary Todd Lincoln
jokes.punchline: 'I need her like I need a hole in the head' — an idiom that, delivered by Abraham Lincoln, is the darkest possible foreshadowing — followed immediately by a gunshot sound ('Bang!')
jokes.explanation: The episode-closing joke and it's a good one. 'I need her like I need a hole in the head' is a common idiom that becomes a horrific pun in the mouth of Abraham Lincoln, who famously received a hole in the head. The 'Bang!' making it literal is the darkest possible button. Well-structured escalation from mild Lincoln-wife annoyance to assassination-joke punchline. High on earned_vs_cheap because the idiom itself does the work, not a forced reference.

tmdb_overview: Andy takes some of the office staff on a field trip to Gettysburg for inspiration. Meanwhile, the rest of the office, under orders from Robert California, are tasked with coming up with a new business idea for Dunder Mifflin. Kevin proposes several ideas that catch California's attention, although they are rather idiotic.
